query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-depositing a thin, conformal high‐entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer on tungsten surfaces before consolidating the W–Cu composite will inhibit phase separation and interfacial void formation during high heat flux and irradiation, thereby improving its thermal conductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite in which tungsten exists either as discrete particles or interconnected ligaments embedded in a copper matrix; this composite exhibits phase separation and the formation of deleterious interfacial voids under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin HEA coating (for example, a CoCrFeNiCu alloy) onto the surface of the W phase via techniques such as electroless plating or sputtering prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: The procedure is carried out during composite fabrication, with subsequent service under high heat-transfer loads and irradiation conditions characteristic of plasma‐facing material joints with Cu-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: The HEA interlayer functions as a diffusion barrier and interfacial mediator, creating a graded, well‐bonded interface between W and Cu that minimizes composition gradients and reduces void nucleation.
generation.mechanism: By providing an intermediate phase with good lattice compatibility and a high mixing entropy, the HEA coating modulates interdiffusion during thermal cycling and irradiation. This suppresses the thermodynamically driven phase separation and the formation and growth of interfacial voids, thereby maintaining a continuous, low‐resistance pathway for heat flow.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA‐coated W–Cu composite will exhibit a higher effective thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite due to improved interfacial bonding and fewer voids, even after exposure to high heat flux and irradiation.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites that show significant phase separation and interfacial voids, which contribute to reduced thermal conductivity under similar thermal and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective within the temperature and irradiation ranges relevant to plasma–facing component joints. However, its performance may be limited if extended to temperatures or radiation doses beyond those typical of the intended fusion reactor environments, or if the HEA coating degrades under extreme conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the HEA interlayer is anticipated to stabilize the interface, uncertainties remain regarding its long-term stability under continuous irradiation and extreme thermal cycling; additional work is needed to optimize coating thickness and composition for endurance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of W–Cu composites with the HEA interlayer applied to the W surfaces and one set without the coating (control). Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation conditions that mimic those at plasma–facing joints. Post-exposure, characterize the interfacial microstructure using TEM/SEM, and measure thermal conductivity, interfacial void density, and mechanical integrity.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (using laser flash or similar techniques) before and after thermal/irradiation exposure
High-resolution imaging of interfaces (TEM/SEM) to quantify void formation and phase homogeneity
Diffraction or spectroscopic analysis to assess phase composition and interdiffusion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after exposure, the HEA‐coated composites do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial voids and phase separation (or fail to yield higher thermal conductivity) compared to the control samples, or if the HEA layer degrades to a state comparable with the untreated interfaces, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents SEM images of the interface structure between the HEA particle and Al matrix in the FSPed AMCs under different heat treatment times. The interface of the composites had a good metallurgical bonding between the HEA particle and matrix (Figure 6a), and only few gray phases marked as Phase 1 in Figure 6b could be observed at the interface, which suggested that little interface reaction between the HEA particle and the matrix metal took place during the FSP. It could be found that a ring-shaped shell zone with a two-layer structure generated around the HEA particle after solution treatment for 2 h (Figure 6c). Upon the solution treatment time increasing from 2 h to 8 h, the thicknesses of the shell zone gradually increased. Once the solution treatment time reached up to 8 h, the core part of small HEA particles ultimately disappeared due to the increase in thickness of the shell zone (Figure 6f). Generally, the microstructure of the shell zone consists of two kinds based on morphologies (Figure 6d,e), which depicts the shell zone as two layers.

The W-based composite having uniformly distributed TiC within the grains and along the grain boundaries can withstand heat flux as high as 200 MW/m2, which is nearly 100% higher than the flux sustained by pure W. An increase in the amount of the evenly distributed TiC in the W matrix (inside the grains and along the boundaries) also increases the hardness creep strength and modulus of elasticity, , . The presence of TiC in the grains and on the grain boundaries also favors fusion applications, as it increases the recrystallization temperature and irradiation resistance. TiC does not have a significant effect on the deuterium retention behavior of W-based materials, . The dispersion of carbides in the grain boundaries of W leads to grain boundary strengthening and provides some resistance to grain boundary migration at elevated temperatures. Therefore, TiC is considered to be beneficial in high-temperature and plasma-facing alloys.
